profile.name: Povrateno
profile.tagline: A women's Macedonian oro from Skopje defined by interlocking belt holds.
profile.insight: In the region of Skopje, women dance the 2/4 rhythm of Povrateno by linking their belts—left hand crossed over right—to step out a medium-fast half circle on whole feet.
profile.profile: Povrateno is a traditional Macedonian folk dance, or oro, originating from the Skopje region. Performed exclusively by women, the dance is characterized by medium-fast movements executed on flat feet. The dancers assemble in a half-circle formation, holding one another's belts with the left arm crossed over the right. Set to a 2/4 meter, it represents the regional tradition of Macedonian collective line dancing.
profile.profile_long:
Povrateno, whose name translates to 'Recovered,' is a traditional women's folk dance, or oro, hailing specifically from the Skopje region of North Macedonia. Entrenched in the regional folklore of the Skopje valley, this traditional line dance highlights the collective movement styles of Macedonian women's dance traditions.

The dance is executed in a half-circle formation. Rather than joining hands, the dancers link together by holding onto each other's belts, placing the left hand over the right hand of the adjacent dancer. The movement is performed at a medium-fast tempo, with dancers stepping firmly on the whole foot. Set to a steady 2/4 musical meter, the dancers progress as a unified unit through the half-circle spatial path.

Historically documented by ethnochoreologist Mihailo Dimovski in his landmark 1977 study *Macedonian Folk Dances* (*Македонски народни ора*), Povrateno serves as a clear example of the structured oro forms found in the Skopje region. The music of North Macedonia provides the rhythmic framework of 2/4 time, supporting the rhythmic stepping pattern of the women's line.

While details regarding specific costume attire are not detailed beyond the functional belt hold, traditional Macedonian oros of the Skopje region typically feature local folk dress suited for line dances. Today, Povrateno remains classified as a foundational Macedonian folk dance within the regional oro lineage.

sections.origins_and_history: Povrateno originates from the Skopje region of North Macedonia. Documented by ethnochoreologist Mihailo Dimovski in his 1977 publication *Macedonian folk dances* (*Македонски народни ора*), it is classified as a traditional Macedonian oro.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by women in a half-circle formation. Dancers hold their belts with the left hand placed over the right hand of their neighbor. The movements are medium-fast and executed on whole feet, stepping to a 2/4 rhythm meter.
sections.music_and_instruments: Povrateno is accompanied by traditional music of North Macedonia set in a 2/4 rhythm.
sections.costume_and_setting: Specific costumes are not detailed in the sources beyond the essential use of a belt, which dancers grip to form the interlocking line.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The name *Povrateno* translates to 'Recovered' in English. It is a traditional regional women's oro, though specific occasion details are not described in sources.
sections.notable_figures: Mihailo Dimovski documented the dance in his 1977 work *Macedonian folk dances* (Skopje: Naša kniga & Institut za folklor).
sections.lineage: Povrateno is a subclass of the Macedonian oro dance family, specific to the Skopje region.

basic_steps: Form a half circle with other women dancers.
Grasp the belts of adjacent dancers with the left hand crossed over the right hand.
Step on whole feet at a medium-fast tempo in 2/4 meter.
teaching.level_notes: Medium-fast tempo executed on whole feet while maintaining an interlocking belt hold.
